query: Consider the following context: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising candidates for next-generation nuclear applications, particularly fusion reactors, due to their excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance. In that context, which material can be used for low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components (PFCs) in fusion reactors, and why?

generation.hypothesis: The refractory high-entropy alloy TiZrHfNbTa can be used as a low-activation structural material for high-temperature plasma-facing components in fusion reactors due to its excellent high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase solid solution with a body-centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure
generation.intervention: Alloying with refractory elements and high-entropy alloy design
generation.conditions: High-temperature (up to 1000°C) and neutron irradiation (up to 10 dpa) conditions
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary cohesion and dislocation density
generation.mechanism: The high-entropy effect leads to enhanced grain boundary cohesion and dislocation density, resulting in improved high-temperature mechanical properties and irradiation resistance
generation.predicted_outcome: A 20% increase in yield strength and a 30% reduction in swelling compared to traditional low-activation structural materials (e.g., F82H) at 1000°C and 10 dpa
generation.boundary: 10% reduction in yield strength or 20% increase in swelling
generation.uncertainty: The actual performance of TiZrHfNbTa may vary depending on the specific alloy composition, processing conditions, and irradiation parameters

falsification_experiment.design: Tensile testing and neutron irradiation experiments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yield strength of TiZrHfNbTa decreases by more than 10% or swelling increases by more than 20% compared to F82H at 1000°C and 10 dpa, the hypothesis is falsified
